definition: At the Newport Festivals (2026), a wristband for one companion of a registered guest; the companion still needs a ticket.
An on-site desk where disabled guests and companions collect access wristbands, as at the Newport Festivals (2026).
Registering a band online so it is tied to you and, where used, a payment card and emergency contact.
A polished recap video released after the festival as year-round marketing.
A UK trade and lobby group for independent festivals that counts closures and lobbies on tax.
Showing the total price, including mandatory fees, from the start; required in the US for live-event tickets since May 12, 2025.
Gate logic that blocks a band from entering twice without an exit scan in between.
Harm to competition as a whole, rather than to one competitor, that a plaintiff must show to win an antitrust case.
UK charity founded in 2000 that sets access standards for live music.
Heavy weights, such as concrete Jersey barriers, that hold a temporary structure down in wind.
An act's position and type size on the poster, which signals status and is negotiated by agents.
The temporary city built each August for Burning Man, which its own Journal describes as closer to a makeshift city than a festival.
Selling festival tickets before any artist is announced; Newport Folk's 2026 tickets sold out within seconds this way.
An on-site balance or currency that only works at that festival, with no cash or card accepted.
All greenhouse gases converted into one carbon-equivalent number.
Policy wording that removes cover for cancellations caused by disease outbreaks; since COVID it has been close to universal for events.
Death from being squeezed so hard that breathing stops; the ruled cause of all 10 Astroworld deaths.
Food, drink and merchandise sold on site; listed by Live Nation as festival revenue alongside camping fees and ticket service charges.
Enough ownership of a company to direct it; Madison Square Garden Co. bought one in Boston Calling Events in 2016.
A portable cell tower on a truck or trailer, brought in by carriers for big events.
People per square meter; UK planning typically uses 2, and about 5 is given as the upper limit for standing.
Chaotic waves of pressure in a very dense crowd that push people off their feet.
US nonprofit founded in 1998 that runs harm reduction booths at events.
The lineup broken out by day, usually released after the full poster.
Decibels weighted to match how human ears hear loudness.
A reusable cup you pay a small deposit on and get part or all of it back when returned; Roskilde's costs 5 DKK and refunds 1 DKK (2026).
A festival people travel long distances for, often sold with travel, such as Tomorrowland's Global Journey packages.
Dour Festival's on-site currency, priced at 1.75 euros each (2026).
Tomorrowland's campsite, which opened on schedule on July 17, 2025, the day after the main stage fire.
Chemical testing of a substance to tell the person who handed it in what it contains.
A band carrying both an NFC chip for payments and a UHF chip for gates.
Prices that change live with demand during a sale.
The cheapest ticket tier, sold first in limited numbers; the price rises when it sells out.
A deposit refunded when you hand in bagged litter; Bestival charged 10 pounds (2018 reporting).
An estimate of the money a festival brings to an area, often commissioned by the festival or a tourism body.
A safety plan and site map Boston's Office of Emergency Management requires for any event with capacity of 1,500 or more.
Glastopedia's name for Glastonbury's pandemic cancellations in 2020 and 2021.
Cover that repays costs or lost income if an event is canceled for a listed reason.
CTS Eventim's live and festival arm, with more than 50 formats across more than 45 promoters.
UK industry body that has published the Purple Guide since 2012.
Official resale of tickets at the original price, through the festival or its ticketer.
A planned year off, used by Glastonbury to rest the land; the festival still has costs and can post a loss.
AIF's proposed UK relief for festivals under 30,000 capacity, modeled on theater and orchestra reliefs.
A barrier running back from the front into the crowd, built to take the same load as the front barrier.
Rhode Island state park on Newport Harbor; home of Newport Jazz since 1981 and Newport Folk since its 1985 revival.
An event with no admission charge; Woodstock and Isle of Wight 1970 were declared free after the gate failed or profit became impossible.
The promoters' argument that a rival festival benefits from an artist booking it did not pay to build; used to defend radius clauses.
A load-bearing steel or aluminum A-frame fence, about 1.2 m high, that holds the crowd back from the stage.
Shorthand for Bob Dylan's plugged-in set with members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band at Newport Folk on July 25, 1965.

aka: Guide to Safety at Sports Grounds
definition: The UK sports ground safety guide, which uses 4.7 people per square meter for standing viewing areas.
A festival built from scratch on open land such as a farm, usually with camping, like Glastonbury or Bonnaroo.
Total ticket revenue before costs; often misreported as profit.
A fixed fee paid to an artist regardless of ticket sales.
The original Health and Safety Executive event safety guide that the Purple Guide replaced.
A renewable diesel made from waste oils and fats that runs in ordinary diesel generators; its emission savings are disputed.
Spending by people who earned money from the festival, such as staff spending wages; counted in multiplier totals.

term: Isle of Wight County Council Act 1971
definition: A UK local law with sections designed to control large overnight gatherings, passed after the 1970 festival.
An average sound level over a set period; the Pop Code uses 15 minutes.
Attitude is Everything's access standard for venues and festivals, introduced in 2022.
Early, sometimes cheaper, access for people who bought tickets or attended in past years.
A festival held on a cruise ship with performers and fans on board, such as Jam Cruise or Holy Ship!.
The 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has produced the Newport Jazz and Newport Folk festivals since 2011; it focuses on music education and artist relief.
Short-range RFID at 13.56 MHz, read at about 4 cm; used for deliberate taps such as payments.
A festival whose surplus goes to a foundation or charity, like Roskilde or the Newport festivals.
The festival's written proposal to an artist's agent, setting the fee, deal type, deposit and payment schedule and logistics; it can become binding once accepted.
A Boston license for live entertainment at a single event, usually the last permit issued.
A wristband closure that can be tightened but not loosened; the only way off is cutting, which voids the band.
Boston's main permit for public events, issued by the Mayor's Office of Consumer Affairs and Licensing (MOCAL) in three tiers.
Insomniac's name for advance EDC Las Vegas passes, sold with a $5 deposit in 2024 before the next lineup was out.
Patients seen by medical services per 1,000 people on site; 13.47 at Glastonbury 2022.
Paying for a festival ticket as a deposit plus later installments.
A UK planning right allowing temporary land use, such as a festival, for up to 28 days a year without full planning permission.
The staffed gap between the front barrier and the stage where stewards, first-aiders and paramedics work.

aka: Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts
definition: The UK's 1995 Noise Council code setting music noise targets at nearby homes for events between 9am and 11pm.
An opening night before the main days, usually with a smaller crowd. Fuji Rock's drew 16,000 in 2025.
A sale window before the general on-sale, for past buyers, sponsor cardholders or a sign-up list.
Investment firms, such as KKR or Providence, that buy companies to grow them and later sell them.
The company that books the acts, secures the site, sells tickets and advertises the event, and takes the financial risk.
The UK's subscription good-practice guide to health, safety and welfare at outdoor events; guidance, not law.
Glastonbury's main stage, first built in 1971 when the event was called Glastonbury Fair.
A contract term barring an artist from public shows within a set distance of the festival for a set period before and after it.
US federal law (2003) cited as making promoters wary of on-site drug checking because of liability.
How some festivals define a wristband: permission to enter that the festival can withdraw, not property you own.
A battery-free chip read by radio when a reader comes close; the basis of festival wristbands.
A setup where acts alternate between adjacent stages; Boston Calling merged its Green and Red stages this way for 2025.
Where an artist's tour already goes; festivals that fit the route are easier and cheaper to book.
A company that bought up dance music promoters in 2012-2013, went public in 2013 and filed for bankruptcy in 2016.
An order for the crowd to stay where it is and take cover until severe weather passes, used at Newport Folk on July 25, 2025.
Festival sound carrying past the site into nearby neighborhoods, as Boston Calling's did across the Charles into Cambridge in 2017.
December to March, when Australian, New Zealand and South American festivals run, such as Laneway in February and Lollapalooza Argentina in March.
A resale listing for a ticket the seller may not yet hold; Newport Folk warned fans against them in 2025.
A base guarantee plus a percentage of ticket sales once the promoter's expenses are recouped.
A sponsor's physical presence on site, such as a branded stage, booth or product sampling.
Crowd and gate work, often done by charity volunteers in exchange for free entry.
A festival group founded in 2017 that runs more than 80 festivals in Europe and Australia; owned by KKR since 2024.
A performer who appears without being announced, a Newport Folk tradition (Dolly Parton in 2019, Joni Mitchell in 2022).
An AIF campaign launched in 2019 against the estimated 250,000 tents left at UK festivals each year.
The person at a festival or promoter who chooses artists and sends their agents offers, usually within a fixed talent budget.
A stage, roof or tower bolted together on site and taken down afterward; UK loading guidance comes from the Institution of Structural Engineers.
Short-term hearing loss after loud noise.
UK nonprofit that runs festival drug checking; first to receive a Home Office festival licence in 2024.
A 2015 Powerful Thinking report benchmarking UK festival emissions at about 100,000 tonnes CO2e a year including audience travel.
Requiring each attendee to register before the sale so the ticket carries their name and photo, as Glastonbury does.
In Boston, an event that runs more than a day, serves alcohol or draws more than 250 people, among other triggers; it needs at least 30 business days' notice.
Grouping acts into font-size tiers and listing them alphabetically within each tier, as Roskilde described in 2019.
A company whose name goes on the festival itself, as with the JVC Jazz Festival in Newport from 1984 to 2008.
The number of toilets per attendee; UK council guidance starts at 1 per 100 women and 1 per 500 men plus 1 urinal per 150 for events open six hours or more.
Adding money to a wristband balance, online before the festival or on site.
One lineup that moves city to city over days or weeks, like Laneway's six-city run in February 2026.
One festival bill that travels from city to city, as Lollapalooza did from 1991 to 1997.
Reselling tickets for profit; touting is the UK word, scalping the US one.
A city tax on hotel and short-term rental stays; a third-party guide lists Indio's at 13%.
Running the same festival on two back-to-back weekends to double the crowd without enlarging the site. Tomorrowland has done it since 2017.
RFID read from about 1-6 m, used at gates to read several bands at once without stopping.
The unique ID number on a wristband chip; the festival looks it up in its own database at each scan.
A shared on-site command bringing in the EMS, fire and police agencies that would answer a 911 call, recommended by the Texas task force in 2022.
A festival held in a city park or venue, usually without camping and sold by the day, like Lollapalooza in Grant Park.
A pledge launched in 2015 asking outdoor events to cut greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2025.
Multiple barrier lines dividing the area in front of a big stage into separate pens.
